subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITY
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS FOR RELEASE OF JAMES CROSS BY KIDNAPPERS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. During the course of last night, police forces undertook an intensive search in order to locate Mr. Cross and his kidnappers as well as the killers of Mr. Laporte.
Following this action, the police received a note from the presumed kidnappers of Mr. Cross calling for discussions between a person designated by them and a representative of the governments. This morning, the representative of the federal and Quebec governments, Mr. Robert Demers, initiated such discussions.
The House will remember that several weeks ago the governments offered those holding Mr. Cross as a hostage a safe-conduct in exchange for his release. The offer still stands, and representatives of the Department of External Affairs are now in Montreal to make arrangements in connection with this safe-conduct, if necessary. The House will understand that, as discussions are now in progress, I cannot give more information at the present time.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Justice Minister (Mr. Turner) or myself will report to the House on any important new development.

Mr. Speaker, ever since the government took office it has led the elderly people of this country to hope for great things. We members know this because we have been receiving delegations, messages and letters from elderly people across the country asking to have their pensions upgraded, pointing out the gap between the cost of living and their pensions, and urging that something be done. Every time delegations came to Ottawa to meet the government they returned home with full hearts and empty hands. They were led to believe that relief was just around the corner, that the government was taking time to make a survey of their needs, what it would cost them to live in a modern way, and that when the package deal was ready they would be everlastingly grateful for having a government which was so considerate of elderly people.

The minister had spoken with approval of the fact that, by cutting off the 2 per cent escalator from the people who would not get the supplement, the government this year would save $15 million and by 1975 would save $100 million in handling old age pensions. That is what the government is saying. As a matter of fact, the minister spoke with pride as though he were a Robin Hood robbing the rich to help the poor, instead of a comfortably insulated cabinet minister compelling poor old age pensioners to finance those who are even poorer.
Why not get this money from the rich? Something else that happened yesterday struck me vividly. When this suggestion was made to the minister I remember the sort of hopeless shrug he gave. As a result, we have automobiles, television sets and all the other advantages of this modern age. They have lived insecure and hard lives. What they are being given today is not enough to live on but too much to die on. If they were not such a hardy breed, they would not survive. This does not say much for us who do this to them.
If the minister would raise his sights he could do more, even under the whip of some sections of public opinion, such as those who are too well off, or under the whip of some sections of the cabinet. A whole new approach of recognition and gratitude is needed for those who built this country. These people need social justice, not handouts. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend this afternoon to make a grandiloquent speech packed with statistics and which might be beyond some hon. members' understanding.
I just want to say that in my opinion the white paper is a masterpiece, all the more so as we have been expecting reforms in social security in Canada for several years.
We need only recall that in November 1962 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked for a reform of social security in Canada. He also asked that old age pensions be increased.
The white paper is a working document and it will be discussed at length at future federal-provincial conferences. It is a reflection of the comprehensive philosophy that is the trade-mark of a forward-looking government which has since 1919 always been ahead of all others in the field of social security.
A short while ago, I heard the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) state that the Minister of National Health and Welfare was suffering from headaches. Those have been caused by the incredible amount of work he has been doing and, for the most part, they are due to the numerous congratulations that have been extended to him.
I spoke with older people last night and this morning, and they are all very happy with this new measure. Not one member, I think, received any phone calls from these people expressing discontent.
I could give you a great deal of statistics, but I shall simply say to support my point that 52 per cent of older people receive a supplement ranging between $1 and $31.83. But of these, 475,000, or 28 per cent, receive the full amount of $31.83.
The underlying principle is fantastic. It is a fairer distribution of wealth. That is why the 2 per cent supplement for the high cost of living was suppressed.
I heard the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) recently say that we will never in this way solve the problem of increasing poverty among the masses. This is true. Surely, when we draft laws, certain boundaries are not easy to determine. Still one must agree that the measure now under consideration will certainly help a great number of people, including those who have served Canada well, as has been so often repeated in this House. I feel that the elderly are satisfied with their lot and that they will send us letters of congratulations. Indeed this bill is not perfect, but it is at least an answer to a certain wish of the people.

December 3, 1970
Old Age Security Act
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
And to come back to the principle of universality, the hon. members for Winnipeg-North-Centre and Vancouv-eir-Kingsway would grant $150 to every aged person, but as in democracy a choice must be made, we have opted for selectively because it is fairer. Pension universality would lead to socialism and entail enormous expenditures.
Those who are not in office may say what they want, and it is a pity because in the process they often show irresponsability.
As for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) he said the program was too modest and not generous enough. He spoke as if he had felt the obligation to say something in the House so that later on he will be able to say that when the bill was introduced, he expressed some criticisms. But I am sure that deep in his heart-and he is a great-hearted man-he supports the measure. He cannot say so openly, because he is the Leader of the official Opposition.
As for our friends of the New Democratic Party who surely show some socialistic tendencies, they cannot understand our attitude and we cannot agree on the administration of the legislation, baceuse their principles are opposite to ours. Indeed, legislating in such a field is not as easy at it is believed. We must not forget also that the funds which we can take out of the taxpayers' pocket are limited. Between two evils, one must choose the lesser. This is why the principle of selectivity rather universality has been chosen.
When we see sick persons, as I do every day, we note that they want to show their gratefulness to governments which thought about them. That is why I am convinced the people of Canada will approve this bill, as well of course as the principles of the white paper, and especially the provisions with regard to family allowances and old age pensions; and also the study that will be made of this document which, to my mind, is a masterpiece.
We are told that we should mind our own business, in the federal government, and leave such programs as that on old age security to the provinces. Yet, it will be remembered that, in 1951, the Canadian government, implementing the recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on old age pensions, proposed to the provinces a constitutional amendment expressly granting Parliament the power to set up a national old age security pension plan to be administered by the government of Canada. The provinces agreed to it and, in 1951, the Constitution was amended accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, I believe what we are doing will be welcomed by the elderly people of Canada, even those who are sitting at home looking at television with nothing else to do but think, eat, rake over their past and look a little toward the future. When we give them more money, they are very happy, not caring about the constitution and the legal problems which might come up when such a bill is introduced. They are concerned with concrete things. When you give a child candy, it appreciates the candy, not because it is made in China, in Russia, in Montreal or in England, but because it is good.
From the practical point of view, discussions should be limited as much as possible to approve such a clever and rational legislation the aim of which is to allow older citizens to become first class citizens who will be able to afford some luxury.
Last Tuesday, that is on December 1st, a woman who had just received her pension cheque, told me that even with the supplement, she had only $13 left at the end of the month. Thanks to the new legislation, she will obtain a great deal more. She will appreciate all the more those who had a thought for her and the other old people who are facing daily problems. As much as possible, we should speed up the process in order to consider other more important matters. Regardless of the amendments made or what is said about this legislation, basically the bill is very good. Once again, the government has demonstrated, without any doubt, that it is forward-looking as far as social security is concerned, as it has always been since 1919.
No other government has done as much in the field of social security as this one. No other government that could succeed it will ever be able to do better. Besides, if it had not been for the federal government, I am wondering where social security would be today? The federal government is often criticized in various quarters, but yet, it is the federal government that has given the breath of life to all Canadians.
It is for that reason that we carrying on our work, regardless of any criticism. Whatever we do, I am sure that we are on the right road. It took many months to prepare this legislation. By adopting it, we shall be of great service to those who look to us, not for discussions, but for bread and butter and a small measure of comfort, in order to spend their last years in comparative well-being.

speechtext:
Mr. Cross is presently on Terre des Hommes, technically in the hands of the Cuban government. Negotiations are being pursued and are being completed for his final liberation. Negotiations are along the line of our undertaking to offer safe conduct to those who were his alleged kidnappers, and these negotiations are proceeding.
I must say that my first reaction is one of joy and relief at these events, and I am sure that all hon. members of this House and the Canadian public share this reaction. In the name of all Canadians I want to congratulate Mr. Cross for his fortitude and his family for their great patience.
I would also add that we are very thankful for the co-operation that existed at all levels between the government of Quebec and our government with regard to this matter. I want to commend the police for their coolness, especially in the final stages of this nightmare. I also thank the Canadian public for their patience throughout.
I believe there is nothing I can usefully add at this stage. I have, as I say, talked to Mr. Cross, and also to the British High Commissioner. I am trying to establish contact with Prime Minister Heath of Great Britain. I repeat that at this stage negotiations are well along toward a useful and final solution to this ghastly nightmare.

I knew Mr. Cross and his wife in Halifax. I knew him as a very fine person indeed, and his wife too. They both have shown very special qualities during these weeks. We have all been feeling very much for them. I sincerely hope that their sufferings are over and that they may be able to join each other very soon.
I do not know whether this would be a proper question, but the Prime Minister indicated negotiations were going on with a view presumably to granting safe conduct for the kidnappers of Mr. Cross. Do these negotiations in any way involve also the kidnappers of Mr. Laporte?

speechtext:
Bill C-202 is to be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Services and certainly I am not going to speak at any length as I wish to see its reference facilitated.
Yesterday my leader and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) both voiced some doubts and some concerns about this legislation. I intend to voice some doubts and concerns. Before emphasizing one or two of my personal concerns in this respect, let me recall a statement made yesterday by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) whom I see standing behind the curtain listening very intently. He said that in his opinion there had been some hair-splitting by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). He went on to say that some of the statements made by members on this side of the House did not make sense and he accused people over here of a certain amount of irresponsibility. I should like to read one sentence of the hon. member's speech made yesterday:
II I were a member of a party that had very little or no chance of ever forming the government, of ever being responsible, I would offer them $1,000 a month.
I think that statement is the height of irresponsibility. It is an indication of how much can be said for the hon. member's arguments concerning universality versus selectivity. This is something I should like to discuss for a moment.
We should consider the different approaches in respect of universality versus selectivity. Perhaps I am thinking out loud at the moment, but back in 1950-51 there was a joint committee of this House and the other place which met for a considerable period of time. The four parties in the House at that time were represented on that committee as well as two parties from the other place. This joint committee brought in a unanimous recommendation as to how we should assist our elderly citizens. Perhaps that was the first time in the history of this country that such a unanimous recommendation was brought forward by such a committee.
That recommendation was to the effect that everybody should receive $40 per month upon attaining age 70 as a right, without any means or needs test. There were certain residence rules, that is agreed. But I repeat that that recommendation was unanimous and I think it was sound. Since then, there have been some upward revisions in the amount paid and there have been some changes in residence rules, some lowering of the age when the payment commenced. As the minister of that department for a period of time, I had the responsibility and the pleasure of sponsoring some of the amendments for consideration in the House. Incidentally, the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned what a God given gift to Canada the Liberal party has been in the field of social welfare. I suggest that our government of that day had
December 3, 1970

an enviable record in the field of social welfare. I suggest also that the claims of the Parliamentary Secretary can simply be labelled outrageous.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
That universality of approach which was recommended back in 1950-51-I think the act came into force on January 1, 1951-continued until very recent times. I think it was a sound approach. Everybody was free to apply for and receive old age security without any stigma attached to it and without any suggestion that it was not their right to receive these funds. Incidentally, I have known individuals in the early days of the Old Age Security Act who would not apply for the pension, even though they were entitled to it. They were too proud to do so. I think, however, that as time went on and people realized they were being taxed through the corporation tax, the sales tax and the personal income tax to pay for old age security, everybody pretty well agreed that this was a sound approach. The receipt of old age security was theirs as of right. A fund was established which, at the end of the last fiscal year, was in the neighbourhood of $725 million.
The guaranteed income supplement came into being in 1966. At that time I recall moving an amendment in this House that all old age security recipients receive $100 a month. I still think that that would have been the right step to take at that time. However, the guaranteed income supplement was chosen, and it does seem to me that Canadians as a whole have now pretty well accepted the principle that those who show need for it should be able to receive monthly payments over and above the basic old age security payment. We all remember the 2 per cent cost of living annual increase in basic pensions, as well as the guaranteed income supplement. But even that was completely inadequate. It was a maximum figure. Since that time the cost of living has increased immeasurably more than that. Most years the increase was double that amount.
Primarily I want to say a few words about the basic pension which is now to be fixed at $80 a month and frozen at that figure. The minister intimated that in 1967 position with regard to comparable return would be restored. This is absolutely incorrect. The minister also, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Macln-nis) pointed out, seemed to want to leave the impression that there will not be any further increases in the cost of living. I say again, that is utter nonsense. The basic figure-if there is going to be a basic figure, and I am not arguing with that-should be at least $85 and more to restore recipients to a comparable position to that of 1967. Instead of that, the minister is making the figure $80. It is 42 cents more than the recipient is receiving as the basic pension this year. But if the pension had kept step with the increase cost of living, it would have been a great deal higher.
Yesterday the minister referred to an abnormal increase in the cost of living over the past few years. It is not abnormal to recipients of old age security. I suggest it is disastrous. Now, that basic figure is to be frozen at $80
Old Age Security Act
a month. I think this is wrong. To be comparable with 1967, it should be considerably higher. There is to be no further escalation on this basic rate due to the increases in the cost of living. The basic pension is going to be frozen forever or, as was indicated earlier, unless there is a change of heart in the government. I suggest there should be a change of government because certainly this is not an adequate figure. Recipients have been taxed to build up this fund. It is their fund, it is their money, and the money is available. There was $725 million odd in the fund at the end of the last fiscal year. If recipients have other income, they will be taxed in the future.
I am concerned about the departure from the principle of universality. I have always felt that the wealthy who receive old age security pensions pay a huge percentage of them back in income tax, but they have paid into the fund originally. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) yesterday outlined the position in which various groups of retired Canadians will find themselves. This was a very interesting and accurate analysis. At the moment, I am concerned with the group of people about whom mention was made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, those 510,000 Canadians who have some other income and who, as a consequence, will not be receiving the guaranteed income supplement because they will not qualify for it. However, their total income will be very small.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
They are going to be limited to the $80 per month. They are not going to be allowed any escalation of that $80 to off-set increases in the cost of living. Mr. Speaker, I think this is wrong. It is wrong to penalize our elder citizens who, over the years, tried to save a little for their retirement, as well as pay taxes, and who are now singled out as not being eligible to receive a cost of living increase.
The government has not fulfilled its promise of a just society. While I agree with some of the provisions in Bill C-202, I point out that it should have been introduced two years ago. As has been so eloquently mentioned today by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, our elder citizens have been suffering untold hardships. They have not been receiving proper attention from governing bodies throughout the country.
Despite huge increases in the cost of living, some 500,000 of our elder citizens will still be penalized. As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of some of the provisions in the bill. Despite my reservations, I urge its rapid consideration on second reading so that it may go to committee and be returned to the House, even though 500,000 people whose pensions are to be frozen at $80 per month would be receiving $81.17 if the legislation were not passed by the first of the new year. Despite this fact, I believe the bill should receive rapid passage simply because of the guaranteed income supplement which is so necessary, and which will mean so much to so many of our elder citizens who are in dire circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to express my opinion about the treatment of our older people in Canada.
We are trying at the present time to improve the Old Age Security Act, but this bill will give older people less security than before. We disagree will the white paper's recommendations and we certainly do not agree with those who say that older people are given a fair treatment, that they receive more than anywhere else, that they can do nothing else but congratulate the government and all the administrators in this country.
I say it is far from being the case, contrary to the claims of certain members or observers.
Every day, like other members, I meet a number of old age pensioners from all over Canada and they ask me whether it would be possible, through discussion with the responsible people, to obtain pension increases, for they cannot make both ends meet. As a matter of fact, 90 per cent of the older people complain that they are in need due to an overly rapid increase in the cost of living. Yet, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) said a while ago that older people were satisfied with their lot and were thanking the present government for being so generous to them.
The government is far from generous. Indeed, it is the older people themselves who built this country, who left us the heritage of progress. In return, they certainly deserve some consideration from the administration.
Mr. Speaker, if we compare what older people receive in Canada with the income other Canadian pensioners get from the government, such as veterans, who receive pensions reasonable enough to allow them to face the cost of living, we find that the old age security pension is far from being equal to that of veterans, for instance.
The pensions paid to widows or orphans and other dependents of ordinary citizens and to older people should be as high as those granted to orphans and widows and other dependents of veterans.
Those who worked to build the country should get the same consideration as those who died on the battlefields to save it.
The pension of veterans' widows is being increased by $240 to $2,640 per annum or $220 per month. But why should not all other citizens be given the same treatment?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, whether a citizen dies at work, on the battlefield or in any other field of social activity, his widow, his children or his dependents remain Canadian citizens, and their social, economic or political needs are still the same. So why not grant the same pensions to the dependents of a deceased ordinary Canadian citizen as those granted to the dependents of a soldier who died in the war or after?
Is the citizen responsible for building houses, manufacturing furniture or tilling the land not as deserving as a
[Mr. Monteith.l
policeman, a seaman, an airman, or a soldier who looks after the security of the Canadian people? Then why not treat in the same manner all the Canadians who look to the government for the bare minimum?
Why does the old age security pension of a veteran amount to $2,640 a year, or $220 a month, while that of an old worker is only $110 a month? I want to know the reason and I want us to discuss it. It is essential to reach logical and specific conclusions and to remove once and for all these differences in income which go against the government's commitments towards our citizens who are entitled to live out of our national production for 1970 and 1971.
Each year our production should help our people to live before being used as a reserve.
That is why this bill which provides $80 per month for older people is illogical. As for us, we see the situation as follows: since the government claims to have found some solutions to check the rising cost of living, it should actually stop increasing. But did the government actually find a truly effective formula to prevent the cost of living from increasing? If they have found one, they should freeze the old age pensions at $80 per month without paying attention any longer to the rising cost of living. But I presume the government is far from having found this magic formula and it is therefore illogical to set the old age pension increase at $80 per month.
The hon. member for Hull stated a moment ago that pensioners will get more generous pensions, that this bill will be beneficial and welcome because inadequate pensions by $30, $32, $33 or $35 a month are being raised. I do not know exactly the amount of this increase, but if the pensions were increased by $20 a month, it would still not be enough since the cost of living has increased four fold in the last few years and keeps on increasing.
Those who now receive benefits are subject to a needs test. All those who get a supplement claim it is not enough. They come and ask us to urge on their behalf the Department of National Health and Welfare to make up the difference. Needs are great because the cost of living is too high. If it keeps on increasing pensions would have to be raised, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, to $150 a month for all older people and this, without a needs test.
In this manner, the government would save on administration costs and we would no longer have old people ask for a supplement, claiming that they are as poor as their neighbours, their fellow-citizens, who also receive a pension. Why punish those who told the truth? Those people have no right to receive a supplement and every day, there is some argument as to whether such and such a pension is entitled to the supplement.
If we want to be logical, we should put an end to such discrimination against older people. If we are fighting to achieve justice then we should hand out every month, without a means test, a sum of $150 to each and every older citizen and, through income taxation, we could take away from the rich whatever surplus they have and distribute it to those who are not so well-to-do.
December 3, 1970

The government should improve on this legislation. In due course, we intend to introduce an amendment to this act, as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, aimed at increasing the pension to $150 per month, which definitely would not be too much in a country as rich as ours.
This year, our surplus amounts to $34 million. We pay western farmers not to grow grain. We penalize eastern farmers to prevent them from producing milk and other foodstuffs. In spite of it all, we tolerate that citizens should go hungry because they do not have the necessary slip of paper to buy all what they need.
We can treat our senior citizens equitably: it only calls for a spirit of social solidarity. Through taxation, we could set up a fund to assist our older people.
We could go further and say that it is as illogical to take money from such places, when other solutions would be possible. Nobody ever thought about that.
Never have we looked into excess profits; never have we looked into the resources of big financial institutions, of large companies, and of hidden reserves which amount to billions of dollars. We could take a few hundred million from these sources to ensure decent security for the aged.
We shall never put enough money in circulation to make our economy viable. Whenever we place money into the hands of people, we do boost the economy; we are exerting pressure on the economy so as to make it increasingly effective. The economy needs transfusions because it is depressed and in the need of injections, a way of placing pressure on the economy to make it operative.
Mr. Speaker, though not a socialist, I strongly support the measures put forward by NDP members. We could however raise pensions without falling into socialism.
The existing capitalist structure revolves around profits and expenses.
Sufficient returns are needed so that, once expenditures are deducted, we are left with profits. This is the formula that we must apply. Then, we will be able to pay everyone what he is entitled to. Aged people will then enjoy a reasonable standard of living in a country which is overflowing with resources. I hope that this formula will be understood by our administrators.
Once this put in practice, we will not have anymore problems, and it will be easy to increase pensions to $150 without any means test, because this is a terrible trial for aged people. The party which he represents, Mr. Speaker, has an excessive concern, in my opinion, with the problems of distribution of wealth. In other parts of the world we have seen the philosophy of the new left in our time expressed. Men like Servan-Schreiber have written very, very ably showing that in contemporary society we must carefully balance policies dealing with the distribution of wealth with policies that go to creating the incentive that will bring about the wealth that is to be distributed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mrs. Maclnnis) and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare took up much of the time of the House today. We apologize for doing so, but I trust it is for the greater good of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, the motion for publication of the report of the findings of the survey team, which under the direction of Dr. H. C. Rowsell inspected university research laboratories across the country and made an assessment of the conditions surrounding the use of animals for experimental purposes was rejected. In fact, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, during the last session, asked the hon. member to withdraw her motion.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot produce the briefs requested by the hon. member because Dr. Rowsell's inquiry was done on behalf of the Canadian Council on Animal Care, a body organized as a standing committee of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. The Association is an entirely independent organization, not a Crown agency. Moreover, the report prepared by Dr. Rowsell is confidential and to divulge its contents would betray the Council's confidence and hinder its relations with research institutions.
I would also like to remind the House of the recent debate on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). The government does not avoid its obligations to ensure that laboratory animals are treated, kept and taken care of in a decent way.
I would like at this stage to point out to the House a recent measure passed by the Ontario Legislature and which deals with the care to be given to animals used for research purposes. This legislation eliminates the dealer in laboratory animals which has been mainly responsible for abuses in that field. I would like to add that with few exceptions, all Ontario humane societies have approved the safeguards prescribed by the Ontario legislation which will put an end to most of the inhuman treatments of animals in the past.
We can hope, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation will serve as example to the other provinces. In Ontario, breeders of laboratory animals and research establishments must obtain a licence and their premises will be inspected. If they do not comply with the regulation, their licence could be repealed. In addition, experimentalise of Animals for Research
tion, breeding and distribution will be submitted to legislative control. Under the act, anesthetics are to be used in all experiments which may cause pain and analgesics have to be administered in the course of post-operational care. The act also requires the creation of committees responsible to see that all necessary care is given animals in research establishments, as was recommended by the Canadian Council on Animal Care. These committees are responsible for coordinating all activities connected with research animal establishments, including care standards, personnel training and steps to be taken to prevent pain. These research projects on animals will have to be supervised by this committee so that the latter can insure that the provisions of the law have been strictly complied with.
Let us now examine briefly the activities of the Canadian Council on Animal Care. At the national level, the Council functions as a sort of external consultant agency to insure that guidelines on care and use of animals in laboratories are uniformly applied. After its setting up in 1968 one of its first initiatives was to punish the handbook entitled Care of Experimental Animals, A guide for Canada. In order to prepare that handbook Dr. Rowsell, former executive director of the Council, made a first assessment of 39 universities, 24 federal government branches or research centres and 17 pharmaceutical laboratories.
The guide was used to evaluate the facilities and techniques employed in research and teaching establishments in Canada.
The care given to animals in those establishments was evaluated by professional groups with experience in the various fields of research, breeding of domestic animals and veterinary science concerned with laboratory animals, including members of the Technical Advisory Committee of the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies. Members of such groups provided their services voluntarily.
The Council also attempts to determine the need for professional and technical specialists in veterinary science concerned with laboratory animals, and intends to make recommendations in this regard, if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Council on Animal Care puts its services at the disposal of government organizations, institutions and persons directly interested in the care and use of laboratory animals. Requests for advice, on the rise because of our close relationship with other national and international associations dealing with animal sciences and animal care have constantly increased.
Progress made up to date by the Canadian Council on Animal Care, through a voluntary system of control, is satisfactory. Not only is such a system bringing in improvements in research and teaching but it also makes sure that public concern and interest for the welfare and ethical use of laboratory animals are dealt with in an efficient and responsible manner by the scientific community.

December 3, 1970
Use of Animals for Research
Mr. Speaker, the fact that people have been more concerned about the care of laboratory animals these last few years, is perfectly commendable. However, in order to understand correctly this greater concern, it is necessary to recognize the existence of several causes and objectives. Among these, it is to be noticed that researchers are concerned about animal care and ways to improve it because they realize that the use of animals in bad condition often alters the results of experiments. Researchers want also to establish a uniform type of animal for the whole range of biological and medical research. In every type of research, the common denominator is good health, in the general sense of the term, and therefore, it is clear that for research purposes, it is necessary to have animals in good shape.
The reports submitted by the assessment groups are considered by a resource group of the Council and discussed and accepted by the Council before being submitted to the designated administrative board of the establishment involved. These reports that the hon. member would like to be made public are confidential. Their findings have always been approved by the directors and the scholars concerned and have led in almost all establishments to the creation of local committees concerned with the experiments and animal care.
The basic principles of the use of animals by first year medical students have been reviewed to encourage the use of less sophisticated animals. The principles specify that no experiments shall be conducted on vertebrates if they injure the normal health of the animals or if they cause them any pains or troubles. These principles were approved by the Foundation of Young Scientists which sponsors scientific exhibitions. Moreover, this Foundation has accepted to ensure a higher degree of supervision on students who use animals for these scientific exhibitions. Projects using animals must be approved, and a responsible supervisor must be assigned to them.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The Council on Animal care is also concerned with increasing the availability and improving the quality of animals to cope with the needs of research and dissemination of information on animal sources in Canada. The needs of regional supply centres, the means to control and licence commercial suppliers, and the compilation and inventory of all types of animals raised in various establishments in Canada have been considered.
The question of the use of laboratory animals raises in the mind of scientific researchers the question of ethics, a question which has been often raised and has been studied for a long time. Ethical pressures on the individual scientist come from his colleagues, from local committees, from a provincial advisory committee or from a national council, to mention only a few of the groups which supply him with money for research and which publish papers.
Therefore, controls already exist to ensure humane treatment of laboratory animals, and they are applied according to the best democratic tradition of this country.
Mr. Speaker, during the last half of this century, many research fields have been suggested, including chemotherapy, virology, endocrinology, radiobiology and medical genetics, while others that were only in their infancy at the beginning of this period, namely immunology, nutrition, biochemistry and applied pharmacology have evolved to such an extent that they are almost unrecognizable.
Before 1900, it was thought that the specific causes for illnesses were foreign to the human body. Today, illness is considered as a functional disorder to which many factors contribute, especially bacteria, viruses and other micro-organisms as well as the receptivity of the system, the nutritional state and professional risks.
Such a new concept of disease has greatly enlarged the scope of biological sciences and therefore greatly expanded the field of biological research and experimentation, the object of which is to prevent or relieve suffering in man and animals.
Perhaps the greatest achievement of the last 50 years in the field of medicine is the progress made in chemotherapy, the treatment of infections by means of drugs. In 1935, the discovery of sulpha drugs made possible for the first time the efficient treatment of bacterial infections. A few years later, a wide and growing field of research on antibiotics was open, due to the evidence of the therapeutic effectiveness of penicillin in bacterial infections. Since the discovery of penicillin, not so long ago, many new types of therapeutic and chemical products have been discovered and used, for instance, for the treatment of such illnesses as diabetes and high blood pressure.
In the field of immunology, science has reached a level of development far above that of the study of defence mechanisms. Today, we are trying to understand body reactions to the invasion of any kind of foreign proteins as well as the problems posed by allergic reactions which seem to be the result of an unfavourable reaction of the body towards its own organs and, more recently, the unfavourable reactions resulting from the grafting of complete organs such as the heart and liver.
In the field of surgery, many breakthroughs over the last few years are a direct result of experiments made on animals. Many of the main achievements in the field of chest, heart or brain surgery are the result of studies on the physiological effects of similar operations performed on animals. The successful use of artificial materials for reconditioning body structures are also based on preliminary experiments made on the performance of those materials in the body of an animal.
Mr. Speaker, we should remember the experiments of Professors Vineberg and Selye of Montreal, who have contributed much to science in Canada through experiments on animals.
These are but a few examples of the fields of medical science which have, as I just said, benefited by research on animals, demonstrating that each step forward in science has been accompanied by an increase in the scope of experiments and the number of specialists qualified to carry them out and therefore of the number of laborato-

December 3, 1970

ries equipped with the necessary research facilities. The need for animals to be used in scientific research is therefore a direct implication of research for scientific knowledge.
When research is geared toward potential applications to humans, the need to use a living animal is subject to fundamental principles of medical ethics. No doctor will proceed with a new method of treating a patient unless he is reasonably satisfied that this new process is or seems to be adequate for relieving his patient, nor unless he is perfectly aware of any potential side effects that he may have to assess professionally as against the benefits of the operation. The information which helps the doctor in making a decision is often enough based on the results of comprehensive studies of the effects of new techniques recommended for operating on animals.
Hence, our conclusion may be that the demand for laboratory animals will continue to increase in the near future and that the development of substitutes for tests on animals will not materially affect the demand for in vivo laboratory animals because in vitro tests do not allow the doctor to acquire the necessary guarantee before trying a new medicine or a new treatment on his patient. Indeed, the expansion of research will bring in more problems as regards proper supplies and care for animals. These are the reasons why the Canadian Council on Animal Care has been established.
People who are frequently required to look after and use animals for scientific research have the moral obligation and the responsibility of directing this research for the benefit of both people and animals. This responsibility consists, partly, in constantly seeking the discovery of proper solutions to the problems arising out of the anxiety or the hazards to which these animals are exposed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that I am convinced that the work of the Canadian Council on Animal Care is the answer to both the ethics and the concerns of society, so that animals used in scientific research be treated humanely. Wherever possible, inferior forms of animal life and insensitive systems are used. However, wherever it is necessary to use superior animals to better the lot of mankind and the animal world, such research is conducted, I am satisfied, in a very humane manner.
Perhaps I should say, before concluding my remarks, that it is thanks to animals that medical science has reached its current level. If animals could understand, we would extend our gratitude to them. It is said that a dog is man's best friend. I am sure that all scientists have the greatest respect for animals, and to an increasing degree, they use humane methods in their experiments.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) before the House this afternoon requests that an order of the House do issue for a copy of the report of the findings of the survey team which under
Use of Animals for Research
the direction of Dr. H. C. Rowsell inspected university research laboratories across the country earlier this year and made an assessment of the conditions surrounding the use of animals for experimental purposes.
The Parliamentary Secretary has outlined many of the reasons why the government cannot produce a copy of this report. First and foremost among these is that this survey was carried out by an agency which is independent of the government. But I think there are many other reasons why it would not be in the best interests to release this report.
The Canadian Council on Animal Care was set up in 1968 because it was recognized that there was a need for better animal care in Canada. The first director of this agency was Dr. Harry Rowsell, a former professor of the Ontario Veterinary College who later became professor at the Western College of Veterinary Medicine in Saskatoon. Dr. Rowsell, whom I know very well, is the most competent person to be the first director and the first man in charge of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
One of his first tasks was to produce a guide on the care of experimental animals, which I am sure people who are concerned about this matter in Canada have read and have found to be a most adequate, initial book on the subject. I am sure that as our experiments on animals become more complicated and sophisticated, this book will be amended and new aspects will be added to it. However, as an initial document for this kind of agency it was and is an excellent text.
The next task that the Canadian Council on Animal Care undertook was a survey of all the laboratories throughout the country, both the research laboratories and those that are operated by drug companies as well as laboratories which are located at universities. I think it should be understood that the survey of these facilities did not only have as its purpose an assessment of the treatment of animals at these laboratories; it also had an educational mission, because the guide had been produced only a year before and such a survey had not been carried out by this type of survey team composed of very capable people travelling across the country to assess these facilities. So I believe the role of this survey team had great educational value for the people operating these research laboratories. I understand that this was done on a voluntary basis but that nearly every laboratory in the country co-operated.
Certainly, as time goes on there will be more sophisticated assessments of research laboratories, and perhaps better regulations. But I think it would be very inappropriate for the first report of the survey team, which contained not only an assessment of animal care facilities and laboratory facilities but also provided an educational role for the people operating these facilities, to be released. I believe that after the survey team visited the various facilities throughout the country, the level of animal care and the kind of facilities provided improved greatly. Since it was voluntary and was done on a confidential basis, I think it would be quite inappropriate for this report to be released.

December 3, 1970
Use of Animals for Research
I expect that at a later stage we will want to establish a regulatory body, whether it be federal or provincial, which will assess these facilities, and if they are not up to a certain standard penalties will be imposed on the laboratories and research establishments concerned. However, I do not think that the overwhelming amount of publicity which would emanate from the publication of this report would necessarily have the best results.
The study of the basic processes of life are fundamental to medical research and to other health science disciplines. Frequently these studies require that research be carried out with animals, and also that living processes be studied as an adjunct to teaching. The benefit which society derives from the use of animals for research and teaehmg is incalculable. As an example I would cite the dramatic decline of poliomyelitis which has resulted from the development of a vaccine, prepared through the use of monkeys, against the virus of this disease. This is best illustrated by the statistics for Canada. In 1959 nearly 1,887 cases of poliomyelitis were recorded; however, in 1969, ten years later, the incidence of poliomyelitis in Canada was reduced to zero through development of the polio vaccine.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The use of living animals for teaching and research is a privilege which is accompanied by responsibility for ensuring that the highest standards of humane care and treatment are provided for animals in our teaching and research institutions. Rapidly expanding scientific research and increased student enrolment in recent years have resulted in increased need for animals. In Ontario alone, in 1967 approximately 636,000 animals ranging from mice to domestic farm animals were used for these purposes. This large use of animals for scientific research, which escalates at between 10 per cent and 20 per cent per year, has necessitated the establishment of more institutions and has sensibilized facilities for animal acquisition, for better accommodation, care and treatment of the animals, requiring the use of professional staff who are especially qualified in respect of animal care.
There are already many programs which provide training and experience in research animal husbandry, and there is a growing emphasis on research into animal diseases and the methods of care, housing and handling of laboratory animals. Research scientists recognize the responsibility for providing the highest standards of care in the accommodation of animals, if for no other reason than that animals used in research and teaching must be in all respects healthy and not subject to environmental or other stresses which could prejudice the results of their studies. To provide animals of the quality necessary for research and teaching, all latent and subclinical diseases must be detected and eliminated by the professional personnel who care for the animals. Facilities must also be constructed to provide research animals with a stable and comfortable environment.
In 1967, a symposium on the care of animals for teaching and research in the life sciences was held at Queen's
University. This symposium, which was sponsored by the faculty of medicine at Queen's, introduced the concept of the Canadian Council on Animal Care, whose objectives are to provide guiding principles for the care of experimental animals in Canada and to work for their effective application. At this symposium Dr. G. Malcolm Brown, chairman of the Medical Research Council of Canada, delivered a paper on the National Research Council report on animal care and the role of the granting agency. In this paper Dr. Malcolm Brown stressed the importance which the Medical Research Council attaches to the care of experimental animals in Canada.
His concern was not only that experimental animals should be treated in a humane manner but, also, that for the purposes of research there is a common basis for good animal care which is not simply a matter of description and definition. Dr. Brown also noted that there was room for improvement in animal care and informed the symposium that scientists are continually seeking improvement in this area.
I shall review briefly the history of the Canadian Council on Animal Care: As early as November, 1963, the Medical Research Council requested the National Research Council to establish a committee to study the situation with regard to the humane use and care of experimental animals. The National Research Council acceded to the request and set up a committee composed of a distinguished jurist, representatives of the two councils, representatives of universities, medical and veterinary schools and a representative of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies.
This committee's terms of reference included a request for recommendations for improvement in the procurement and production of experimental animals, facilities for their care and control over experiments. The work of this preliminary committee was carried out thoroughly under the able chairmanship of Dr. W. H. Cooke, director, division of biosciences, National Research Council, and was the subject of a special report published by the National Research Council in June, 1966. In large measure the recommendations contained in Dr. Cooke's report resulted in the establishment of the Canadian Council on Animal Care. This body, which acts in an advisory capacity, seeks to ensure the development and use of satisfactory practices. In addition, it is the vehicle for proving and exchanging information on animal care.
At the provincial level the committee recommended the establishment of an advisory board which would concern itself with all facets of the problem of animal care, including procurement, production and care of experimental animals. The committee recommended at the provincial level that the registration and licensing of dealers in laboratory animals be instituted where present arrangements were unsatisfactory. Mr. Speaker, this of course has been carried out in the province of Ontario under the legislation which was passed last year.
At the local level the committee recommended that institutions establish their own committees on animal care, with responsibility for ensuring that generally accepted principles were followed within their laborato-

December 3, 1970

ries. Perhaps the most significant finding of the committee was that in its opinion voluntary controls would be more effective than legislative controls in ensuring that improper experimentation did not occur. In arriving at this recommendation the committee examined legislation relating to animal care in various countries and decided that effective control rested in large measure on the judgment of the individual investigator and that of his colleagues, both immediate and remote. The committee concluded that this type of check is the major influence even when there is controlling legislation. Moreover, there are situations which no legislation can foresee or provide for, and an alert and informed attitude must remain the most effective check on the use of animals, as indeed it does in Canada today.
The concern of society for the care of experimental animals is just one part of the examination which society is making of its many activities. Democracy is a system of checks and balances, and it is right and proper that from time to time it should receive the attention of those outside medical and scientific research. The National Research Council and the Medical Research Council by their actions, which have led to the Canadian Council on Animal Care, have left the individual investigator vulnerable to a wide range of comments and pressures. These pressures come from his colleagues, local committees, provincial advisory boards and the national council, to say nothing of the groups which provide the money for his research and which publish his papers. This is a method of control in the best of democratic traditions.
It may be useful at this moment to review briefly some of the elements involved in the use of animals in research. When a new chemical is isolated or developed that promises to be of value to man, it is tested in animals before it is applied to the human body. In many instances the chemical structure of the new substance can be ralated to a particular pharmacological activity, and with this foreknowledge a definite screening plan can be initiated. However, in some instances where the pharmacological interest is in a group of chemically similar compounds about which there is little knowledge, the research approach may be a blind one in the first instance. For the safety of man, such preliminary research must begin with animals.
Generally, the initial screening of new chemicals is done with small animals such as rodents, because of their size, their availability and reproducibility; and because they are relatively inexpensive, these early tests are frequently conducted with rats, mice or guinea pigs. Moreover, their short life span affords an ideal opportunity to follow the effects of treatment in its entirety. For some aspects of research, certain animals are more suitable than others. For example, rats and mice will retain oral doses that many non-rodents reject. Hamsters are ideal for research on mucous membrane because the cheek-pouch of this animal provides an ideal area for testing the healing properties of solutions intended for use on such tissue in humans. Rabbits have relatively large body areas and rather sensitive skin, which makes them excel-
Use of Animals for Research
lent subjects for testing how irritating chemicals may be. It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that while the term guinea pig is properly associated with experimentation, these creatures are not widely used for experimental purposes.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
When administering test material to animals, the investigator attempts to determine the lethality of the chemical, its effects, side effects and range of efficacy. Administration of the material may be oral, subcutaneous, cutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous or it may be administered in some other way. If the researcher knows the intended use of the substance in man, he will attempt to emulate administration of the substance. After initial tests with rodents or rabbits have supplied data on the nature and toxicity of the compound under investigation, if these have been fruitful, more elaborate studies can, if necessary, be devised.
It is at this stage that the larger animals are employed. These more advanced studies are usually conducted longitudinally over a period of time that may be from six months to two years or even longer. Small animals are rarely used for long-term studies because their smallness makes it difficult to follow weight gain or loss with any degree of accuracy. Another aspect in the selection of animals for research is age. In some experiments mature animals are needed, while in others the young are necessary in order to follow growth patterns as they develop.
As I have already mentioned, the smaller the animal generally the shorter the life span, so with the smaller animal researchers are able to go through the whole life span in a relatively short period. They can then judge the effects upon a human who has a much longer life span. Because of possible genetic effects to offspring from compounds ingested by parents, tests may be designed to cover several generations, in which case fertility and reproductive patterns will be examined.
In recent years some uncommon research animals have been introduced into the research laboratory because of special characteristics which make them especially suitable for certain types of studies. These include fish, reptiles, birds and farm animals. Animals having certain personality characteristics, such as aggressiveness, may be used in testing tranquillizing drugs and changes in the personality of the animal in response to these drugs would be studied. This may be very useful for drugs which could be used for Members of Parliament, because some of them are very aggressive. We could determine by the study of aggressive types of animals whether they would be especially useful in humans at a later stage.
As the previous speaker has already stated, and as I mentioned earlier in this speech-

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose tonight in this budget address is to set down in a concise manner the economic strategy of the government for achieving our first economic objective-a steady and substantial improvement in the real income of Canadians everywhere. I propose to go about this task in the following way.
First, I will describe the economic and financial situation as it has developed to the moment. Second, I will discuss the measures we have taken since the last budget in March and the measures we now propose be taken to guide the economy onto a course of high and sustainable economic expansion and full employment. Finally, I will chart the route onto this course as we envisage it for the economy in the balance of this fiscal year and through the next.
A steady and sustainable improvement in the standard of living of all Canadians requires the fullest possible utilization of the nation's human and material resources. It also requires that all regions, sectors and groups of people share in economic expansion; that we progressively narrow regional economic differences; and that we obtain a progressively more equitable distribution of the goods and services we produce.
It is often stated that we must also reach for economic stability, a good price and cost performance, and a satisfactory balance of payments. I see these conditions as means to the end, not the end in themselves. We are concerned about the balance of payments, exchange rates and trade because we cannot hope to reach a steady improvement in the prosperity of our people without satisfactory performance in these areas. Similarly, we are concerned about reasonable economic stability because without it efforts to achieve our primary objective will be frustrated. In brief, our only ultimate concern is for the well-being of all our people. Our other concerns are significant only in so far as they contribute to or detract from this goal.
On October 13 I gave the House a rather detailed account of economic developments this year. I shall not repeat that account tonight. I do wish, however, to draw attention to a number of key features of the situation and to new information which has become available since I last reported.
Of prime importance is the fact that employment is rising in Canada and unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis appears to be falling. This underlying improvement is suggested in the statistics for September and October after allowing for normal seasonal patterns. There may yet be month-to-montih fluctuations from the trend.
The national accounts for the third quarter also reveal that real output in the economy is rising. The pause in the growth of production of goods and services which marked the second quarter did not continue, and this latest information confirms that the economy is now advancing again, although the advance would be stronger if major labour disputes were not in progress.
We are in fact having a considerable boom in housing in Canada, owing in substantial measure to the effectiveness of government policy. Housing starts reached the quite extraordinary level at the annual rate of 270,000 in October. We shall not have a record year for housing in 1970 because of the lower rates of starts in the first part of the year, but it will be a satisfactory year especially when viewed in conjunction with the unusually high level of starts of last year. It is worth noting that the growth in starts currently in progress is concentrated in low income housing in regions of the country where the need is great and where employment growth has been sluggish.
The latest figures on capital investment apart from housing are also stronger and the recent preliminary survey of capital investment intentions indicates growing strength in this area of activity next year, although this year activity in this sector has been one of the weaker elements in our economy.
The year 1970 will go into the records as our best year ever in international trade. The increase in our exports especially in the early part of the year was very vigorous, and perhaps more important the latest figures suggest that this new level of exports is being well sustained. Our merchandise trade surplus for the first ten months of the year was at an annual rate of $2| billion. The current account of our balance of payments, including trade in services as well as goods, will show a record surplus this year. This condition is reflected in the

several months. None the less, the government now feels that it would be appropriate to add to them the stimulus of a variety of yet further measures.
Some of these measures are directed toward the immediate needs of the winter ahead. Others are intended to reinforce existing policies and ensure that the economic pick-up in sight for the year ahead will be both strong and sustained. They will also be directed in large part to those regions of the country where unemployment is highest, and to those groups in our society whose incomes are low. I should like now to outline briefly these new proposals, and to refer as well to the fiscal implications of certain other major policy developments which will also have a stimulating effect upon the national and regional economies in the year ahead.
The first of the new measures relates to unemployment insurance. As hon. members know, the objectives and proposals for fundamental reform of the unemployment insurance system were set out in the White Paper tabled last June by my colleague, the Minister of Labour. I am confident that we are well on the way to a vastly improved system of unemployment insurance, providing substantially better protection for all workers in Canada. Because of the time required for consideration and implementation of the new system, however, it is not expected that the higher levels of benefit can be introduced until about next July.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In the meantime, therefore, the government has decided that there should be an immediate increase of 10 per cent in the rates of benefit under the existing system.
This supplementary allowance would be provided to all workers receiving the insurance allowances during the period January to June next. It would be financed by a special government contribution to the insurance fund at a total cost of $54 million. I am sure this increase will be particularly helpful to unemployed workers and then families, especially during the usual seasonal winter peak in unemployment. It will, as well, give an immediate and direct stimulus to the economy, the benefits of which will spread quickly right across the country.
A second new measure proposed is to give still further aid to the provinces, and through them to municipalities if the provinces should so decide. This will take the form of assistance in the financing of additional job-creating public works. A fund to help stimulate the economy will be set up to operate during the remainder of this fiscal year and 1971-72. A total sum of $150 million will be provided by way of long-term loans at favourable interest rates.
The distribution of this fund to the provinces will be based upon a formula which takes account of their differing levels of unemployment experienced over the las t six months of 1970. Because of their population size and current unemployment problems, the largest amounts will be made available to the provinces of Quebec and British Columbia. Based upon our estimates, however, all provinces will be able to make claims upon this fund as a

source of finance for clearly identified capital projects initiated before the end of calendar 1971.
We will, of course, seek the co-operation of the provinces to ensure that projects are undertaken quickly. Wherever appropriate, these projects will be co-ordinated with the existing development programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which in co-operation with the Department of Finance and other federal agencies will administer this loan program.
The projects should be additional to whatever would have been planned for 1971, or they should require financing that would have been beyond the provinces' borrowing capacity. A number of provinces advise us that they have important projects which they would like to move forward quickly in order to create new jobs and economic activity. This additional financing will make this help possible.
In making provision for this fund, we took carefully into account the special submission by the Prime Minister of Quebec to the federal-provincial conference of last September. That submission dealt with the question of evening out fluctuations in provincial revenues over good times and bad. It was agreed at the conference that federal and provincial ministers of finance should give further study to joint efforts to improve fiscal stability. The government's response in this regard as outlined today is directed to the immediate needs in the year ahead. We would plan, however, to continue to explore with the provinces the whole concept involved in possible joint stabilization arrangements for the future.
The federal government itself, of course, is also responsible for a wide range and variety of important capital works across the country. As a third measure of added stimulus, therefore, it is intended to allocate a further sum of $23 million to departments and agencies to undertake further capital improvements in regions where unemployment is most severe. This is a follow-up to the earlier decision announced in October to add $60 million to departmental spending. The review of programs undertaken in that connection indicated a further range of important needs that had been deferred because of the shortage of budgetary funds. It is now proposed to take further steps to reduce this backlog of requirements. Wherever possible this work will also be initiated this winter, continuing where necessary into the next fiscal year.
Parallelling this expanded capital program carried on by federal departments, a fourth program is also planned to accelerate the development of access roads and necessary local services in the area surrounding the new Montreal International Airport. Parliament has already provided substantial funds for construction of the airport itself. Work is getting into high gear on this major project. It will proceed rapidly throughout the year ahead. Services throughout the surrounding municipal areas must also be progressively developed if the region is to achieve its full potential as a dynamic centre for economic growth in the province and the country as a whole. A sum of $20 million of contributions to these needs will
December 3, 1970

therefore be allocated through the special areas program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
A fifth measure proposed is to provide immediately a further amount of $40 million to the capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As I have already recalled, the corporation's budget was raised by $100 million last August to enable it to expand its lending for construction of moderate cost homes for home ownership and rental accommodation for families of modest incomes. The response to this initiative has been remarkably quick. It is apparent that the corporation's program is filling a real and urgent need. As before, it is intended that the bulk of these additional funds should be directed to areas where housing and employment needs are greatest. This additional appropriation will help not only to assure a very high level of housing starts but also to strengthen the round of economic activity that accompanies the creation of new family homes.
Accompanying these direct government programs, three further steps to stimulate the flow of investment in the private business sector are proposed. The most important of these will be presented shortly to the House by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, but I should like to describe here very briefly the main highlights. Certain important amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act will be proposed. If they are approved by Parliament they will be followed by the designation of a new region within which a special system of capital incentive grants will be applied to encourage new private investment. This new region will include the three countries of relatively slow growth m southeastern Ontario-Stormont, Glengarry and Prescott-and the southwestern part of Quebec, including Montreal, which is not now designated.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The development incentives will be available within this new area for a specific time period. We believe they will bring to more rapid fruition many investment projects which would not otherwise be likely to materialize for some time.
It will also be proposed that the present ceiling on incentive grants for individual projects in the Atlantic provinces should be raised, and that a new system of loan guarantees to assist in the financing of viable new enterprises in all the designated regions should be established.
As I have suggested, the details of these important extensions of the industrial incentives program will be made known shortly. They will go into effect as quickly as possible, although it will be some time before their cost will be reflected in our expenditures. It is also very difficult to predict the volume of investment likely to be effected or the probable cost of the incentives. Judging from experience with the program to date, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion foresees a total increase in outlays because of the new program amounting to about $130 million over the period of the next few years. Incentives of this magnitude certainly provide a powerful forward thrust to increased private capital

investment and the creation of jobs throughout the designated regions. The new system of loan guarantees will reinforce that effect.
The other two measures to maintain and expand employment in the private sector directly are aimed at particular industries. One of these is the shipbuilding industry. As recently announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, a carefully designed program of further assistance to Canadian shipyards over the next year and a half is to be introduced to help our companies improve their competitive position and expand sales in strong world markets. We intend to provide the financial support required and we look to the industry to continue to diversify and increase its efficiency in serving both domestic and foreign markets. It is estimated that this program may cost upwards of $60 million over the next several years.
The other situation relates to the footwear industry, which is facing exceptional problems of adjustment. It is proposed that the provisions of the General Adjustment Assistance program should be extended to firms in this industry which require financial and technical aid to restructure their operations in order to improve their competitive position.
Both of these industries tend to be labour intensive. They are also located to a considerable degree in slower-growing regions of the country where unemployment is highest. They are, therefore, industries uniquely fitted to receive selective measures of support at this time.
Supplementary estimates covering several of these measures will be tabled in the House tomorrow morning.

In this over-all review of economic stabilization policy, I should also recall several other areas of expenditure of particular relevance to the expansion of the national economy in the course of the year ahead.
Last Monday the Minister of National Health and Welfare tabled the government White Paper on Income Security. Apart from its signficance as a social document, its proposals have important fiscal and economic implications which are likely to be widely debated. For the moment, however, I need only note the fact that beginning on April 1 next the proposed boost in the combined old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement up to the level of $255 per month for a needy couple will raise total federal payments by almost $200 million over the fiscal year. Under the proposed plan it would not be necessary to raise the taxes earmarked for old age pensions since the yield of these taxes appears adequate to finance the new system. Moreover, a plan along the lines suggested in the White Paper to restructure family allowances, that is, restricting them to families with incomes below $10,000 annually, more than doubling them for families in the lowest income brackets, and making the allowances taxable, would redistribute the expenditure toward needy families in a very significant way.

December 3, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Benson
I should also recall yesterday's announcement by the Minister of Veterans Affairs regarding veterans' pensions and allowances, involving a net increase in expenditure of about $25 million next year.
Changes in our major social programs are clearly directed to the lower income groups in our society. They are also of greater relative importance to the weaker regions in the country. One can be sure that the great bulk of the expenditure will quickly work its way into the consumer spending stream. The impact of these long-planned measures of social justice will thus come just at a time when it is desirable to stimulate demand in the economy not only for purposes of the short-term economic upturn but also for continuous and sustained economic growth.
Much the same stimulus would flow from new government proposals in quite a different area. I refer here to the grain receipts stabilization plan outlined to the House five weeks ago by the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. If that plan is enacted and
